story: After a content word in flowing prose, the circuit predicts the short function word or comma that links the phrase to what comes next, regardless of topic.
The circuit predicts the determiner or light punctuation (the/a, comma, hyphen, newline) that opens or separates the next phrase in any running text.
In text with repetitive structure, the circuit predicts closing punctuation or a short function word that has already occurred earlier in the same context.

The circuit supplies the next piece of a multi-token proper name, compound, or technical term, usually a word-internal continuation with no leading space whose completion is fixed by the name itself (often seen earlier in the context).
Inside long list-like sentences, the circuit predicts the comma or coordinating function word that separates or joins the enumerated items.
After a completed subject noun phrase, the circuit predicts the linking word (a copula like 'is' or a preposition like 'to') or the period that closes the clause.
The circuit continues abbreviated or coded strings such as URLs, postcodes, figure labels and identifiers, producing the short fragment or abbreviation the code-like pattern requires.
The circuit predicts the article or short function word that opens the next noun phrase in ordinary prose sentences.
In descriptive second-person prose, the circuit predicts the frequent function word (especially 'the', 'a', 'you') that continues the sentence after a prepositional or verbal lead-in.

When a word is split mid-token (inside URLs, identifiers, or long names), the circuit predicts the lowercase word-internal continuation, typically copying the same word from an earlier occurrence in the context.
The circuit predicts the coordinating connective, most often ' and', that joins clauses or list items and keeps a long sentence going.
After a noun or pronoun, the circuit predicts an apostrophe continuation: possessive 's, contraction 'll, or a bare quote mark.
The circuit reproduces the next token of a boilerplate template that occurred earlier verbatim in the context, such as listing punctuation or repeated code declarations.
The circuit predicts the second element of a two-part compound or collocation: either the hyphen inside a hyphenated compound or the content noun that completes a familiar noun-noun pair.
Within a repeated formatting pattern, the circuit predicts the delimiter (space, semicolon, comma, paren) or short function word that the established template requires next.
The circuit copies the exact whitespace, newline, or punctuation token from an earlier identical passage; it is near-pure induction on formatting tokens in structured text.
At the end of a complete descriptive sentence, the circuit predicts the closing token, usually the period, or the newline/semicolon that terminates the line.
The circuit performs strict verbatim copying: it predicts the next token of a sequence that has repeated exactly earlier in the context (map-listing punctuation, markdown headers, category lines).
Immediately after its host word or line, the circuit predicts a word-attached suffix or line-ending token: a contraction like 's/'re/'ll, sentence-final punctuation, or the newline closing a heading.
The circuit predicts the high-frequency punctuation or function word that continues running text, reusing tokens already common earlier in the same context.
